grammar.title: Grammatik
grammar.rule: im Zimmer · an der Tür · auf dem Stuhl · in einer Kiste · in einer Dose

tables.caption: der, die, das · dem, der, dem

grammar.note_en:
This chapter describes location: where a person, object or activity is situated. German marks these location phrases with the dative case. You already know nominative for subjects and accusative for direct objects; dative is another form used here after the location prepositions. Compare der Stuhl (“the chair”) with auf dem Stuhl (“on the chair”), die Tür (“the door”) with an der Tür (“at/on the door”), and das Bett (“the bed”) with auf dem Bett (“on the bed”). Masculine and neuter definite articles become dem; feminine becomes der. Der can therefore be masculine nominative or feminine dative: follow the noun and its job, not the article in isolation.

The indefinite article has einem for masculine and neuter, einer for feminine. The story shows auf einem Tisch (“on a table”), in einem Regal (“in a shelving unit/on its shelves”), in einer Kiste (“in a box”) and in einer Dose (“in a tin”). These articles belong to the location phrase. They do not change an earlier direct object into dative: Mira nimmt die Dose (“Mira takes the tin”) still has an accusative object. Ein Heft liegt in der Dose (“A notebook lies in the tin”) instead locates the notebook. No dative personal pronouns, dative possessives or dative plural noun endings are introduced here.

Im is the usual contraction of in dem: im Zimmer (“in the room”), im Hof (“in the courtyard”). The earlier fixed im Haus (“in the house”) now joins this general pattern. Am contracts an dem: am Fenster (“at the window”). Feminine an der stays two words: an der Wand (“on the wall”). The same prepositions can later introduce a destination with different case marking; that contrast comes next chapter. Do not decide case merely from whether a verb suggests movement. Here Ich suche in einer Kiste (“I search in a box”) locates the search; its location takes dative even though searching is an activity.

In places something inside an area or container. Auf marks support on a surface. An can mark attachment to a vertical surface, or conventional positions such as at a door or window. Unter means “under,” neben “beside,” hinter “behind,” vor “in front of,” and zwischen “between.” The chapter shows Die Kiste steht zwischen dem Regal und dem Tisch (“The box stands between the shelving unit and the table”); each noun after zwischen has its own dative article. Die Dose steht hinter der Kiste (“The tin stands behind the box”) and Sie ist auch neben der Bank (“It is also beside the bench”) locate the same tin from different reference objects.

Drinnen and draußen mean “inside” and “outside” without requiring a following noun phrase: Mira ist im Zimmer, drinnen (“Mira is in the room, inside”), Emil steht draußen (“Emil stands outside”). Im Hof identifies a particular place; draußen gives the broader inside/outside contrast. A Hof is the paved courtyard here; the Garten is the separate planted garden beyond it. Bank here means a bench for sitting.

Liegt means “lies/is lying” for a flat or resting object: Ihr Buch liegt auf dem Bett (“Her book lies on the bed”). Sitzt means “sits/is sitting”: Mira sitzt auf dem Stuhl (“Mira sits on the chair”). Hängt means “hangs/is hanging”: Der Schlüssel hängt an der Tür (“The key hangs on the door”), Ein Bild hängt an der Wand (“A picture hangs on the wall”). Their dictionary forms are liegen, sitzen and hängen; the vocabulary/card surfaces are the finite forms actually read. Steht continues to describe upright objects or standing people. These are location states, not instructions to place the objects somewhere.

Eine Seite fehlt means “A page is missing.” The torn stub and absent leaf in the notebook distinguish missing from a page that is present but blank. The characters find the notebook in the tin but do not find the absent page or identify who removed it. Their search changes location from the bedroom to the kitchen and courtyard; finding one object creates a new unresolved question.
